QUESTION OF THE WEEK - December quarter inflation data will be released on Janaury 29 and it is seen, along with wages data due in early February, as the key to whether there will be another rate cut in 1997.
To get an idea of expectations, economists were asked for their inflation forecasts. These may change slightly over the next week as they are fine-tuned in the lead up to the data.

The better than expected inflation performance through 1996 gave the Reserve Bank the room to ease rates on three occasions in the second half of last year, and economists are optimistic that the good news will continue into 1997.

The CPI is expected to show the effects of the two rounds of mortgage cuts delivered in the middle of 1996 -- the first prompted by competition in the mortgage market and the second following the first official interest rate cut on July 31.

Subsequent official rate cuts, on November 6 and December 11, will not have an impact on the December quarter result because of the lag involved in the cuts being passed onto consumers, economists said.

However, they will ensure that the CPI remains off the markets' worry list through 1997. The only cloud on the inflation horizon was that some saw a danger that inflation would be starting to rise by the end of 1997.
Underlying inflation is not expected to match the moderation of the CPI, mainly because the impact of the interest rate cuts is removed from the underlying rate.

However, given positive signs from partial price indicators such as import and manufacturing prices, economists expect it will be comfortably within the the lower half of the RBA's two to three percent target band, and remain there through 1997.

MERCHANDISE IMPORTS - After rising in the each of the last four months, the imports bill is expected to have held steady in December. There are no lumpy items, such as aircraft, expected in the data, but those going for a rise cited investment forecasts and increased competitiveness as a result of the rise in the Australian dollar as supporting factors. However, as annual growth remains sluggish -- a flat result would see import levels down by 1.1 percent over calandar 1996 -- economists said a fifth consecutive rise would not necessarily be a sign for concern. Those forecasting a fall pointed to the slower pace of demand, high inventory levels and the likelihood of a corrective
fall after four months of rises.
